sop_title: A sample lockout/tagout policy for your workplace
summary: This policy protects employees who service or maintain machines and equipment by shutting down, isolating, and locking or tagging out hazardous energy before work begins. It also covers removing locks and re-energizing equipment, energized testing, contractor work, shift changes, alternative methods, training, and annual inspections; authorized employees run it, with supervisors enforcing it and the company handling training, surveys, and inspections.

sections.title: A sample lockout/tagout policy for your workplace
sections.reason: Title and table of contents only; it contains no actions.

sections.title: Purpose
sections.reason: States the policy's intent and defines service or maintenance; there is no sequence of actions.

sections.title: Scope
sections.reason: Defines who is covered and which energy types apply; there are no actions.

sections.title: Employer and employee responsibilities
sections.reason: The responsibility statements could be listed in any order; only the restart prohibition is used, as an exception on the lockout step.

sections.title: Lockout and tagout devices
sections.reason: The device criteria could be rearranged freely; the 'recognize who attached it' rule supports an exception on device removal.

sections.section: Lockout and tagout devices (Electrical energy sources)
sections.title: Electrical energy sources
sections.reason: A single requirement with no order; it gates where the lockout step occurs for electrical sources.

sections.title: Exposure survey
sections.reason: The survey must come before each task is evaluated for lockout/tagout, so reversing them breaks the meaning.

sections.title: Energy control procedures
sections.reason: Contains two numbered sequences (lock out before work, release before re-energizing) where reordering, for example verifying before isolating, would be unsafe.

sections.title: Specific energy-control procedures
sections.reason: States that equipment-specific procedures exist and points employers to templates; it describes no actions.

sections.title: Special lockout/tagout situations
sections.reason: A container heading with no text of its own; its subsections are classified separately.

sections.title: Energized testing
sections.reason: A numbered sequence: clearing the area must come before removing locks, and re-locking must come before verifying, so order matters.

sections.section: Special lockout/tagout situations > Contract service and maintenance
sections.title: Contract service and maintenance
sections.reason: Its two sentences could be swapped, but 'before the contractor does onsite work' ties the procedure exchange to a point in the flow.

sections.title: Group lockout
sections.reason: A single applicability rule with no internal order; it becomes a decision gating the lockout step.

sections.section: Special lockout/tagout situations > Shift changes and long-term shutdowns
sections.title: Shift changes and long-term shutdowns
sections.reason: Its two requirements could be reordered, but they are tied to the shift-change and long-term-shutdown points in the flow.

sections.title: Alternative methods
sections.reason: Mostly design requirements in no fixed order, but the risk assessment explicitly gates method selection, so those actions are mapped.

sections.title: Training
sections.reason: The training bullets could be reordered, but 'before assignment', 'annually', the retraining triggers, and record keeping tie actions to points in the flow.

sections.title: Inspections of written energy-control procedures
sections.reason: The inspector must review and verify the procedure before deficiencies can be found and corrected, so order matters.

processes.name: Conduct hazardous-energy exposure survey
processes.trigger: Company implements the lockout/tagout policy and needs to identify affected equipment and tasks
processes.outcome: A survey of affected machines, energy types and magnitudes, and service tasks, with each task evaluated for lockout/tagout

processes.name: Lock out equipment for service or maintenance
processes.trigger: An authorized employee must service or maintain equipment that could expose them to hazardous energy
processes.outcome: Equipment is shut down, isolated, locked or tagged out, and verified de-energized so service work can begin
sections: Lockout and tagout devices (Electrical energy sources)

processes.name: Remove lockout and re-energize equipment
processes.trigger: Service or maintenance work on locked-out equipment is complete
processes.outcome: Lockout/tagout devices are removed and the equipment is re-energized with all workers clear

processes.name: Perform energized testing or positioning
processes.trigger: An energy-isolating device is locked or tagged and it is necessary to test or position the equipment
processes.outcome: The test or positioning is done, and the equipment is again locked or tagged out and verified de-energized

processes.name: Coordinate contractor onsite work
processes.trigger: A contractor is to perform onsite service or maintenance work
processes.outcome: Company and contractor each know the other's lockout/tagout procedures, and company employees comply with the contractor's procedures
sections: Special lockout/tagout situations > Contract service and maintenance

processes.name: Continue lockout through shift change or long-term shutdown
processes.trigger: Lockout/tagout must continue when work shifts change or during a long-term shutdown
processes.outcome: Lockout/tagout stays in place across the shift change or shutdown, with devices monitored during long-term shutdowns
sections: Special lockout/tagout situations > Shift changes and long-term shutdowns

processes.name: Select an alternative energy-control method
processes.trigger: Lockout or tagout is not used for, or prevents completion of, tasks that are routine, repetitive, and integral to production
processes.outcome: An alternative energy-control method is selected from a risk assessment and implemented, with the individual keeping exclusive control of the protective mode

processes.name: Train employee before assignment
processes.trigger: An employee who may be exposed to hazardous energy is to be assigned
processes.outcome: The employee is trained for their role (authorized or affected/area) and a training record with name and date exists

processes.name: Retrain employee
processes.trigger: The annual retraining date arrives, or job assignment, procedures, equipment or process hazards change, or the employee does not follow energy-control procedures
processes.outcome: The employee is retrained and the training record is current

processes.name: Inspect energy-control procedures annually
processes.trigger: The annual inspection of energy-control procedures is due
processes.outcome: A documented inspection (equipment, date, employees, inspector), with any deficiencies corrected and employees retrained

risks.process: Lock out equipment for service or maintenance
risks.what_could_go_wrong: An employee services equipment with several energy sources. Because the group lockout procedure is not written, one source is left unlocked or one worker's lock is not part of the group, and the equipment starts up while someone is inside.
risks.cause: Special lockout/tagout situations > Group lockout requires 'group lockout procedures' but never describes them, and the list of equipment that requires them is an unfilled placeholder ('[Identify the machines and equipment]'). D2 'Yes' has no next step.
risks.impact: Risk of serious injury from unexpected start-up on the most complex equipment. This is also a compliance gap under 1910.147.
risks.severity_reason: Multi-source equipment is exactly where isolation errors are most likely, and the consequence is physical harm.

risks.process: Lock out equipment for service or maintenance
risks.what_could_go_wrong: The verification check shows the equipment still has energy. The SOP gives no instruction, so the employee may troubleshoot under partial isolation or start work anyway.
risks.cause: Energy control procedures step 6 requires verification but gives no handling for a failed check (see the S8 exception in the map).
risks.impact: Service work may begin on equipment that is not de-energized, with exposure to electrical, mechanical, or stored energy.

quantified_impact.metric: Steps that must be complete before work begins
quantified_impact.basis: Energy control procedures, 'before they begin service or maintenance work'

risks.severity_reason: A failed verification is the last barrier before exposure, and leaving it unhandled turns a near-miss into an injury.

risks.what_could_go_wrong: The employee who attached a lock has left the site or ended their shift. A coworker or supervisor cuts or removes the lock without confirming that person is clear, and the equipment is re-energized while they are still exposed.
risks.cause: Lockout and tagout devices requires that anyone can recognize who attached a device. The SOP gives no procedure for removal when that employee is unavailable (see the S13 exception).
risks.impact: Unauthorized lock removal is a leading cause of LOTO injuries and an OSHA citation item.
risks.severity_reason: This happens routinely at shift ends, and the consequence is physical harm.

risks.process: Lock out equipment for service or maintenance
risks.what_could_go_wrong: An affected employee who was away from the area never hears that the machine was shut down or is about to be re-energized, so they try to run it or walk into it during start-up.
risks.cause: Energy control procedures steps 1 ('Inform all affected employees') and re-energize step 2 ('Inform coworkers') give no method and no confirmation that everyone was told.
risks.impact: Affected employees may try to restart locked equipment or be in the area at re-energization.
risks.severity_reason: Verbal notices are easily missed. Other controls (locks, S11 area clearing) reduce but do not remove the exposure.

risks.what_could_go_wrong: Locks are removed for a test and nobody records who removed them, when, or whether they were put back. Equipment is left energized after the test while others believe it is still locked out.
risks.cause: Energy control procedures says temporary removal is allowed only 'for the time required' and 'the procedure must be documented', but it names no form, owner, or time limit. Energized testing steps 3–5 do not mention documentation.
risks.impact: Equipment may be left energized with no lock while work resumes. The required documentation is also missing at inspection.

quantified_impact.metric: Documentation requirements with no stated form or owner
quantified_impact.basis: Energy control procedures, temporary removal paragraph

risks.severity_reason: This is the one point where locks are deliberately removed, and without a record the restore step relies on memory.

risks.what_could_go_wrong: After re-locking, the control check shows the equipment still energizes. The SOP does not say whether to stop, re-isolate, or escalate, so work may resume anyway.
risks.cause: Special lockout/tagout situations > Energized testing step 6 requires verification but gives no failure handling (see the S20 exception).
risks.impact: Workers may return to service work on energized equipment.
risks.severity_reason: This is less frequent than routine lockout, but the consequence is the same exposure to hazardous energy.

risks.what_could_go_wrong: A contractor arrives and starts work before either side has shared its lockout/tagout procedures. Company employees then do not know which locks or rules apply.
risks.cause: Special lockout/tagout situations > Contract service and maintenance requires mutual awareness 'before the contractor does onsite work' but names no owner, method, or record.
risks.impact: Mixed crews may follow incompatible practices. There is no evidence that the exchange happened.
risks.severity_reason: This is likely whenever contractor work is scheduled at short notice, and the impact is confusion over energy controls.

risks.what_could_go_wrong: The contractor's procedure is weaker than the company's, or it conflicts with it (for example on lock types or group lockout). Company employees are told to comply with it and nobody decides which rule wins.
risks.cause: Contract service and maintenance says company employees 'must understand and comply with the contractor's energy-control procedures' with no review or conflict handling (see the S23 exception).
risks.impact: Company employees may work under inadequate energy control.
risks.severity_reason: Conflicts between practices are common, and the default of deferring to the contractor can lower protection.

risks.process: Continue lockout through shift change or long-term shutdown
risks.what_could_go_wrong: At shift change the outgoing employee removes their lock before the incoming employee applies theirs. The equipment is briefly unprotected, or the next shift does not know it is locked out.
risks.cause: Shift changes and long-term shutdowns refers to 'specific written procedures' for continuing lockout, but they are not included in the SOP (see the S24 exception).
risks.impact: Lockout can lapse between shifts, which risks injury and a compliance gap.
risks.severity_reason: Shift changes happen every day, and a lapse in lockout exposes workers directly.

risks.process: Continue lockout through shift change or long-term shutdown
risks.what_could_go_wrong: The one person assigned to monitor locks during a long-term shutdown is absent or leaves, and a tampered or removed lock goes unnoticed for the rest of the shutdown.
risks.cause: Shift changes and long-term shutdowns assigns monitoring to a single '[Employee's name or job title]' (placeholder not filled), with no backup and no monitoring frequency.
risks.impact: Equipment may be unprotected for an extended period without anyone knowing.
risks.severity_reason: Long shutdowns make absence of the single monitor likely, and an undetected lock removal is a direct hazard.

risks.what_could_go_wrong: No one is actually named to do the survey and it is never redone. Tasks judged not to need lockout have no stated alternative control, so they are performed unprotected.
risks.cause: Exposure survey leaves the surveyor as a placeholder, gives no timing or review cycle, and D1 'No' has no next step.
risks.impact: Equipment or tasks needing lockout may be missed, which undermines every downstream process.
risks.severity_reason: This is a one-time foundation activity, so it is less frequent, but gaps propagate to all lockouts.

risks.what_could_go_wrong: A production supervisor decides a routine task can skip lockout and uses an unverified control circuit. No qualified person signs off the risk assessment or the circuit design before workers rely on it.
risks.cause: Alternative methods requires a risk assessment and an ANSI B11.19 circuit but names no assessor, approver, or record.
risks.impact: Workers may rely on control circuitry that does not provide protection equal to a disconnect.

quantified_impact.basis: Actors on S26–S28 in the map

risks.severity_reason: Alternative methods apply to routine, repetitive tasks, so exposure is frequent and an inadequate design is a direct hazard.

risks.what_could_go_wrong: Staff read one section saying control circuits never isolate energy and another allowing control circuits as safeguarding, and they apply the wrong rule to an electrical source.
risks.cause: Lockout and tagout devices (Electrical energy sources) says 'Electrical control circuitry does not effectively isolate hazardous energy'. Alternative methods permits control circuits that are 'as effective as a mechanical disconnect'. The two are linked only by a 'See also' cross-reference.
risks.impact: Employees may lock out at a control circuit instead of the disconnect, or may reject a valid alternative method.

quantified_impact.metric: Sections giving different rules for control circuits
quantified_impact.basis: Lockout and tagout devices (Electrical energy sources); Alternative methods

risks.severity_reason: The cross-reference partly reconciles the two rules, but misreading it on electrical equipment is plausible and hazardous.

risks.what_could_go_wrong: A new or transferred employee is assigned to service equipment before training is finished, because nothing checks the training record at assignment.
risks.cause: Training requires training 'before assignment' but names no trainer, record keeper, or check at assignment. The S30 and S33 actors are unnamed.
risks.impact: Untrained employees may perform lockout, which is an injury risk and an audit finding.

quantified_impact.basis: Actors on S30–S33 in the map

risks.severity_reason: Assignments change frequently, and an untrained authorized employee is a direct hazard.

risks.what_could_go_wrong: Annual retraining dates lapse unnoticed, and the change-based triggers (new assignment, procedure change, new hazard, non-compliance) are never reported to whoever trains.
risks.cause: Training lists an annual cycle plus 4 change triggers but no owner who tracks due dates or receives trigger notices.
risks.impact: Employees work with expired or outdated training.
risks.severity_reason: Without tracking, lapses are likely. The impact is a compliance gap with indirect safety exposure.

risks.what_could_go_wrong: The annual inspection of some procedures is skipped, or it is done by someone who uses the procedure, because no owner schedules inspections or checks inspector independence.
risks.cause: Inspections of written energy-control procedures assigns the inspection to the company and requires an independent inspector, but it names no scheduler and no independence check.
risks.impact: Procedures go unverified, which is an OSHA periodic-inspection finding.
risks.severity_reason: Missing inspections is likely when there are many procedures, and the impact is mainly compliance with indirect safety effect.

risks.what_could_go_wrong: An inspection finds a procedure is not protecting employees, but retraining and the procedure fix have no owner or deadline. Work continues under the deficient procedure.
risks.cause: Inspections of written energy-control procedures says employees 'must be retrained and the procedure's deficiencies corrected' with no owner or due date.

quantified_impact.metric: Corrective actions with no owner or deadline

risks.severity_reason: Findings are infrequent, but leaving a confirmed deficiency open is a serious exposure.

recommendations.label: digitize
recommendations.proposed_change: The surveyor records each machine, its energy sources and magnitudes, and its service tasks in an Exposure Survey register (SharePoint list) through a Power Apps form. Each entry links to the equipment's specific energy-control procedure.
recommendations.reason: The survey becomes a single maintained equipment list that the lockout log, inspections, and group-lockout list can reference. The process owner must also name the surveyor role.
implementation_steps: Process owner names the surveyor role and fills the placeholder in the Exposure survey section.
Create SharePoint lists 'Equipment' and 'Survey Tasks' with columns for equipment ID, energy types, magnitude, task, LOTO required (Y/N), group lockout (Y/N), and procedure link.
Build a Power Apps canvas form for surveyors, usable on a tablet.
Add a review date column, plus a view that shows entries older than the owner-set review interval.

impact.basis: Estimate: time saved compiling and retrieving survey results. No steps or handoffs are removed from the map.

recommendations.label: keep_human
recommendations.proposed_change: A qualified person continues to evaluate whether each task needs lockout/tagout and records the decision in the survey register. The process owner defines what happens on D1 'No' (for example, route the task to Alternative methods).
recommendations.reason: Hazard evaluation is a safety judgment.
implementation_steps: Process owner writes the D1 'No' handling into the Exposure survey section.
Add a 'Control method' choice column (LOTO / Alternative method / Not applicable with justification) to the Survey Tasks list.
recommendations.suggested_tool: Human decision recorded in SharePoint list

impact.basis: No automation; this keeps a human safety judgment.

recommendations.process: Lock out equipment for service or maintenance
recommendations.label: digitize
recommendations.proposed_change: The authorized employee opens a lockout record in a mobile LOTO Log app (equipment, energy sources, lock IDs, owner, group lockout flag). A flow then posts the shutdown notice to the area's affected employees in Teams. This supplements, not replaces, the in-person notice and the physical tag.
recommendations.reason: It creates a live record of who attached which lock. That record supports removal, shift change, and monitoring, and gives the shutdown notice a trail.
implementation_steps: Create a SharePoint list 'Lockout Log' (equipment lookup to Equipment list, lock IDs, authorized employee, start time, status, group lockout Y/N, area).
Build a Power Apps mobile app with a 'Start lockout' screen that pre-fills energy sources from the Equipment list.
Add a Power Automate flow triggered when an item is created: post an adaptive card to the area Teams channel and @mention the affected employees for that area.
If group lockout is Y, show the group lockout procedure link and require all participating employees to be added to the record.
Keep the in-person notice and physical tags mandatory; state this in the app.
recommendations.suggested_tool: Power Apps + SharePoint + Power Automate (Teams connector)

impact.basis: Estimate: time spent locating affected employees. The handoff after S3 remains but becomes tracked.

recommendations.process: Lock out equipment for service or maintenance
recommendations.label: keep_human
recommendations.proposed_change: Shutdown, isolation, stored-energy release, and lock/tag application stay physical tasks done by the authorized employee. The process owner writes the missing group lockout procedure and the group lockout equipment list.
recommendations.reason: These are physical safety actions that cannot be automated, and the group lockout gap must be closed in the SOP.
implementation_steps: Process owner writes the group lockout procedure and fills in the equipment list in Special lockout/tagout situations > Group lockout.
Flag group lockout equipment in the Equipment list so the LOTO Log app (A3) displays the procedure.
Process owner defines handling for energy-isolating devices that cannot accept a lock.

impact.basis: No automation; this keeps human physical safety steps.

recommendations.process: Lock out equipment for service or maintenance
recommendations.label: digitize
recommendations.proposed_change: The authorized employee still physically verifies zero energy, then records Pass/Fail in the lockout record. 'Fail' keeps the record out of 'Ready for work' status and alerts the supervisor, following a stop-work rule the process owner defines.
recommendations.reason: This gives the failed-verification branch a defined, recorded next step.
implementation_steps: Process owner writes failed-verification handling (stop, re-isolate, escalate to supervisor) into Energy control procedures.
Add a 'Verification result' field and a 'Ready for work' status to the Lockout Log.
Add a flow condition: if the result is Fail, send a Teams alert to the area supervisor and keep the status at 'Not verified'.

impact.basis: Adds a control rather than saving time; it depends on A3.

recommendations.label: automate
recommendations.proposed_change: The authorized employee taps 'Start release' on the lockout record. A flow posts the removal notice to the affected employees and closes the record when re-energization is confirmed. The in-person notice continues.
recommendations.reason: It tracks the removal notice and closes the log, so the log always shows current lockouts.
implementation_steps: Add a 'Start release' button and a 'Re-energized' confirmation to the LOTO Log app.
Flow on status change to 'Releasing': post an adaptive card to the area Teams channel.
Flow on 'Re-energized': set the record to Closed with a timestamp.

impact.basis: Estimate: time spent finding coworkers. The handoff after S10 remains but becomes tracked.

recommendations.label: keep_human
recommendations.proposed_change: Clearing the area, checking controls, removing locks, and re-energizing stay with the authorized employee. The process owner adds a procedure for removing a lock when the employee who attached it is unavailable.
recommendations.reason: These are physical safety actions, and removal by someone other than the lock owner needs a defined human authorization.
implementation_steps: Process owner writes the absent-employee lock removal procedure (contact attempt, supervisor verification, notification before return) into Energy control procedures.
Use the Lockout Log owner field (A3) to identify and contact the employee who attached the lock.

impact.basis: No automation; this keeps human physical safety steps.

recommendations.label: digitize
recommendations.proposed_change: Before removing locks for a test, the authorized employee logs a temporary removal against the lockout record, with the reason and planned duration. A flow notifies the area and escalates if the locks are not reapplied by the planned time.
recommendations.reason: This meets the SOP's 'procedure must be documented' requirement and enforces 'only for the time required'.
implementation_steps: Create a SharePoint list 'Temporary Removals' linked to the Lockout Log (removed by, reason, planned minutes, removed at, reapplied at, verified).
Add a 'Temporary removal' screen to the LOTO Log app.
Build a flow on item creation that notifies the area and waits until the planned time.
If 'reapplied at' is empty after the planned time, alert the employee and then the supervisor.

impact.basis: Estimate: time saved on paper documentation. It adds a timed control.

recommendations.label: keep_human
recommendations.proposed_change: The test, re-lockout, and verification stay with the authorized employee. The process owner defines what to do when verification after re-lock fails.
recommendations.reason: These are physical safety actions, and the failure branch needs a human stop-work rule.
implementation_steps: Process owner writes failed re-verification handling into Special lockout/tagout situations > Energized testing.
Record reapplication and the verification result in the Temporary Removals list (A8).

impact.basis: No automation.

recommendations.label: automate
recommendations.proposed_change: When a contractor job is registered, a flow sends the company's LOTO procedures and an acknowledgment request to the contractor and asks them to upload their own procedures. The job shows 'Not cleared for onsite work' until both sides have acknowledged.
recommendations.reason: It makes the 'before onsite work' exchange trackable and evidenced.
implementation_steps: Create a SharePoint list 'Contractor Jobs' (contractor, contact email, start date, company procedures sent, contractor acknowledged, contractor procedures uploaded, cleared status).
Build a flow on item creation that emails the company procedure documents with a Microsoft Forms acknowledgment and upload link.
Update the status when the acknowledgment and upload are received.
Send a reminder to the job owner if the start date is near and the status is not cleared.

impact.basis: Estimate: time spent chasing procedure exchange. The 2 handoffs remain but become tracked.

recommendations.label: ai_assist
recommendations.proposed_change: When the contractor uploads its energy-control procedure, an AI step summarizes it and lists differences from the company procedure (lock types, group lockout, verification). The list goes to a safety reviewer, who decides.
recommendations.reason: Comparing two procedure documents is reading work. AI flags likely conflicts, but the decision stays human.
implementation_steps: Trigger a flow on file upload to the Contractor Procedures library.
Use the AI Builder 'Create text with GPT' prompt with both documents to produce a structured difference list.
Save the output to the Contractor Jobs item and assign a review task to the safety reviewer.
Label the output 'AI draft – verify against source'.

impact.basis: Estimate of reviewer reading time saved.

recommendations.label: keep_human
recommendations.proposed_change: A named safety reviewer resolves any conflict between contractor and company procedures before company employees work under the contractor's controls.
recommendations.reason: Deciding which energy controls protect employees is a safety judgment.
implementation_steps: Process owner adds conflict-resolution handling to Contract service and maintenance (for example, the more protective rule applies).
Record the reviewer's decision on the Contractor Jobs item.

impact.basis: No automation.

recommendations.process: Continue lockout through shift change or long-term shutdown
recommendations.label: digitize
recommendations.proposed_change: The outgoing employee transfers the lockout record in the LOTO Log app to the incoming employee, who acknowledges after applying their own lock. The physical transfer follows the written procedure, which the process owner must add.
recommendations.reason: It gives the shift-change transfer a record, so lockout ownership never lapses unseen.
implementation_steps: Process owner writes the shift-change and long-term-shutdown procedures into the SOP.
Add a 'Transfer' action to the LOTO Log app that requires the incoming employee's acknowledgment.
Build a flow that alerts the supervisor if a transfer is unacknowledged after the owner-set window.

impact.occurrence: per shift change with active lockout
impact.basis: Adds a control; no time saving claimed.

recommendations.process: Continue lockout through shift change or long-term shutdown
recommendations.label: automate
recommendations.proposed_change: A scheduled flow sends lock-check tasks for each open long-term shutdown to the designated monitor, and to a named backup if the check is missed. It alerts the supervisor if any device is reported disturbed.
recommendations.reason: It removes the single point of failure and sets a monitoring rhythm.
implementation_steps: Process owner names the monitor role and a backup, and sets the check frequency.
Add a 'Long-term shutdown' type and monitor/backup fields to the Lockout Log.
Build a Recurrence flow that sends an adaptive card check to the monitor, escalates to the backup if there is no response, and logs results to a 'Shutdown Checks' list.

impact.basis: Estimate: time saved on manual check logging and follow-up.

recommendations.label: keep_human
recommendations.proposed_change: The risk assessment, method selection, ANSI B11.19 circuit design, and personal control stay with qualified people. The process owner names the assessor and approver and reconciles the electrical-control-circuit wording.
recommendations.reason: These are engineering and safety judgments that must not be automated.
implementation_steps: Process owner names the assessor and approver roles in Alternative methods.
Process owner clarifies how the electrical-sources rule and the Alternative methods rule relate.
Store signed assessments in a SharePoint library linked to the Equipment list.

impact.basis: No automation.

recommendations.label: automate
recommendations.proposed_change: When an employee is added to a role that may be exposed to hazardous energy, a flow checks the training register. If no current record exists, it alerts the supervisor and trainer that the employee may not be assigned yet. Training delivery stays human.
recommendations.reason: It enforces 'before assignment' with a check.
implementation_steps: Create or identify a SharePoint 'Role Assignments' list (or use an HR feed if one exists).
Build a flow on new assignment that looks up the Training Records list (A17) by employee and role type.
If no record exists, notify the supervisor and trainer in Teams and create a training task.

impact.basis: Estimate of manual record lookup time.

recommendations.label: digitize
recommendations.proposed_change: The trainer records each completed training in a Training Records SharePoint list (name, date, type authorized/affected/area, trainer) through a form.
recommendations.reason: It provides one searchable record that the assignment check and retraining reminders can use.
implementation_steps: Create a SharePoint list 'Training Records'.
Build a Power Apps or Microsoft Forms intake for trainers that writes to the list.
Name the record-keeper role in the Training section.
recommendations.suggested_tool: Microsoft Forms or Power Apps + SharePoint

impact.basis: Estimate of filing and retrieval time.

recommendations.label: automate
recommendations.proposed_change: A scheduled flow flags employees whose last training is approaching 12 months and assigns retraining to the trainer. A Forms-based 'retraining trigger' report covers assignment, procedure, hazard, and non-compliance changes.
recommendations.reason: It gives the annual cycle and the 4 change triggers a tracked owner.
implementation_steps: Build a Recurrence flow that queries Training Records for last date older than 12 months minus the owner-set lead time.
Create a Planner task for the trainer and notify the employee and supervisor.
Create a Microsoft Forms 'Retraining trigger' form that creates a retraining task.
Escalate overdue items to the supervisor.

impact.basis: Estimate of manual tracking time.

recommendations.label: automate
recommendations.proposed_change: Completing the retraining task writes the new training date to the employee's Training Records row automatically.
recommendations.reason: It removes a separate manual record update.
implementation_steps: Build a flow on Planner task completion (or the trainer form submission) that updates the Training Records item.

impact.basis: S35 manual record update replaced by flow; minutes are an estimate.

recommendations.label: automate
recommendations.proposed_change: An annual flow per procedure creates an inspection task, asks the coordinator to assign an inspector, and warns if the chosen inspector is listed as a user of that procedure.
recommendations.reason: It makes sure every procedure is inspected each year by an independent inspector.
implementation_steps: Add a 'last inspected' date and a 'users' field to procedure records in the Equipment list.
Build a Recurrence flow that creates Planner tasks for procedures due within the owner-set lead time.
Add a condition that flags the assignment if the inspector is in the procedure's users field.

impact.basis: Estimate of scheduling time.

recommendations.label: keep_human
recommendations.proposed_change: The inspector continues to review the procedure with employees and to judge its accuracy, completeness, and effectiveness.
recommendations.reason: Observation and judgment of safety practice must stay human.
implementation_steps: Inspector records the findings in the inspection form (A22).

impact.basis: No automation.

recommendations.label: digitize
recommendations.proposed_change: The inspector documents each inspection in a Power Apps form with the 4 required fields (equipment, date, employees, inspector) plus findings, saved to an Inspections list.
recommendations.reason: It provides complete, consistent inspection records for audit.
implementation_steps: Create a SharePoint list 'Inspections' with the 4 required fields, findings, and a 'deficiency found' Y/N field.
Build a Power Apps form with required-field validation.
Update the procedure's 'last inspected' date on save.

impact.basis: Estimate of documentation time.

recommendations.label: automate
recommendations.proposed_change: When an inspection records non-compliance, a flow creates retraining tasks for the named employees with an owner and a due date.
recommendations.reason: It gives the 'must be retrained' requirement an owner and a deadline.
implementation_steps: Build a flow on Inspections item creation where 'deficiency found' = Yes.
For each employee in the inspection, create a Planner retraining task for the trainer with a due date set by the process owner.
Write completions to Training Records.

impact.basis: Estimate of follow-up time.

recommendations.label: automate
recommendations.proposed_change: A flow creates a corrective-action task for the procedure owner, tracks it to closure, and escalates overdue items.
recommendations.reason: It gives the 'deficiencies corrected' requirement an owner and a deadline.
implementation_steps: Build a flow on Inspections item creation where 'deficiency found' = Yes that creates a Planner task for the procedure owner.
Send weekly reminders until the task is closed, and escalate to the safety lead after the owner-set due date.

impact.basis: Estimate of follow-up time.

starter_flows.trigger: SharePoint – When an item is created in the 'Temporary Removals' list (submitted from the LOTO Log app before locks are removed)
actions: Get the linked Lockout Log item (equipment, area, authorized employee).
Post an adaptive card to the area Teams channel: 'Locks temporarily removed for energized testing on [equipment] by [employee]'.
Delay until removed-at plus planned minutes.
Get the Temporary Removals item again; check whether 'reapplied at' is filled.
If it is empty, send a Teams alert to the authorized employee, wait the owner-set grace period, and if it is still empty alert the area supervisor.
When 'reapplied at' and 'verified' are filled, update the Lockout Log status back to 'Locked – verified' and post a restore notice to the channel.

starter_flows.trigger: Recurrence – at the check frequency set by the process owner
actions: SharePoint – Get items from Lockout Log where Type = 'Long-term shutdown' and Status = 'Open'.
For each item, post an adaptive card to the designated monitor asking: 'Are all lockout/tagout devices on [equipment] intact? Yes/No, with notes and photo'.
If there is no response within the owner-set window, send the same card to the named backup monitor.
If there is still no response, alert the supervisor.
If the response is 'No', immediately alert the supervisor and the safety lead in Teams.
Create an item in the 'Shutdown Checks' list with the equipment, responder, time, result, and notes.
SharePoint – Get items from Training Records where last training date is earlier than today minus (365 days minus the owner-set lead time).
For each employee, create a Planner retraining task assigned to the trainer with the due date = last training date + 12 months.
Send a Teams notice to the employee and their supervisor with the due date.
For items past the due date with no completed task, escalate to the supervisor and flag the record as 'Overdue'.

(Companion flow) When a 'Retraining trigger' Microsoft Forms response is submitted for an assignment change, procedure change, new hazard, or non-compliance, create the same Planner task for the trainer.
